messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adaeze is a 43-year-old Nigerian-American woman who works in IT support and has been married for eleven years. She came to the clinic after her PCL-5 score of 55 prompted a referral from her primary care physician, though she had been carrying what she described as "this weight" for most of her adult life. The events that gave rise to that weight began in childhood, in a rural setting outside Lagos where she spent summers with an aunt and uncle before her family emigrated. The abuse occurred across several seasons, administered by the uncle in an outbuilding surrounded by dense bush and tall grass, the air thick with the smell of red earth and vegetation. He would lock the door behind them. Adaeze remembers the particular quality of silence in that room — the way the outside sounds of insects and wind in the trees were muffled, the way the light came in only through a single high window. She was told, repeatedly, that she brought it on herself by being difficult, by being the kind of child who invited trouble. She was eight years old the first time.

Adaeze has come to believe, with a conviction that feels to her less like an opinion and more like a fact she has simply always known, that there is something fundamentally wrong with her — not something that was done to her, but something intrinsic, a flaw woven into her character that made her the kind of person the abuse could find. She does not frame this as a belief she holds; she experiences it as a truth she lives inside. This deep appraisal of herself as inherently defective keeps her nervous system in a state of chronic readiness. Her body, she says, never quite settles. At her desk in the IT support office, she sits with her shoulders drawn up toward her ears without noticing, and when a ticket comes in marked urgent she feels a spike of alarm that seems disproportionate even to her. She has difficulty concentrating on the step-by-step troubleshooting her job requires, losing her thread mid-task, and she is aware that her colleagues have noticed. She was passed over for a team lead position last year, and though nothing was said directly, she suspects it was because she seems distracted and unreliable.

The chronic physiological tension and the false alarms that fire through her body throughout the day have, in turn, deepened her conviction that something is wrong with her. She interprets her own reactivity as further evidence of her defectiveness — normal people, she reasons, are not like this; the fact that she is confirms what the uncle told her. This loop has been running quietly for decades, each spike of alarm feeding back into the story she carries about who she is.

The appraisals also shape what she can and cannot approach in the world. Because she understands the abuse as something her character attracted, the triggers that are most potent for her are those that place her back inside the conditions of that original scene. A walk in a park or a green space — something she encounters on her lunch break when colleagues suggest eating outside — can stop her mid-stride. The smell of damp earth or the sound of wind moving through leaves pulls the past forward in a way that feels less like remembering and more like return. Confined spaces are worse: if a server room door closes behind her during a maintenance call and she hears the latch engage, her body responds before her mind can intervene, heart rate climbing, chest tightening, the old silence of that outbuilding pressing in. She has begun routing her support calls to avoid rooms without propped-open doors. Talking about the events directly — which she has never done in any therapeutic context — remains almost entirely foreclosed. The body's alarm, once triggered, also makes these situations harder to leave behind; the residual tension from a false alarm at work can linger for hours and make the natural environment on her evening commute feel newly threatening.

What finally brought Adaeze in was a moment three months ago when she was locked briefly inside a server closet after a door malfunction. She sat on the floor for twenty minutes before someone heard her. She has not been able to enter that room since. What she is most afraid of, she says, is that the therapy will confirm what she already suspects — that the problem is not what happened to her, but what she is. What she is most hoping for, though she can barely say it aloud, is that someone will tell her she is wrong.
